content: Exclusive and mixed breastfeeding practices have been shown to contribute to improved health outcomes in infants and toddlers. Research has demonstrated that breastfeeding is associated with a reduced risk of atopic dermatitis in children up to 42 months of age, as evidenced by a birth cohort study conducted in Japan. Additionally, breastfeeding has been linked to higher intelligence quotient (IQ) scores in children aged 4 and 11 years, as well as better early childhood outcomes when breastfeeding exclusivity is maintained. Studies have also highlighted the relationship between breastfeeding and infant body mass index (BMI) peaks, as well as its influence on body composition at age 3. Furthermore, breastfeeding has been associated with a decreased risk of breast cancer in women carrying BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations, as well as a reduced risk of epithelial ovarian cancer. Breastfeeding duration has also been linked to a lower prevalence of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children. In terms of oral health, prolonged breastfeeding has been associated with a lower risk of early childhood caries, although other feeding habits may also play a role. Breastfeeding has been shown to protect against respiratory infections, asthma, and allergies in children, particularly in those with a family history of atopy. Moreover, breastfeeding has been associated with improved cognitive, language, and motor development in children, as well as better educational outcomes at later ages. Breastfeeding has also been linked to maternal health benefits, including a reduced risk of osteoporosis, improved bone mineral density, and a lower likelihood of developing metabolic syndrome. Additionally, breastfeeding has been associated with a decreased risk of type 1 and type 2 diabetes in children and adolescents, as well as a protective effect against childhood obesity. Overall, the evidence underscores the significant shortand long-term health benefits of breastfeeding for both mothers and children, emphasizing its role in promoting optimal growth, development, and disease prevention.
